procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Chief Presidency Magistrate, Calcutta
procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate dated March 20, and June 8, 1967 discharging the accused-appellants.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Some of the office bearers of the first appellant challenged the orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate issuing summons and search warrants in Criminal Revision No. 19 of 1967, praying for quashing the complaint. A Single Judge stayed proceedings, issued summons to the State and the complainant, and ultimately dismissed the Criminal Revision on February 24, 1967, noting that the complainant conceded that offences under sections 337 and 338 of the Indian Penal Code were not made out, but suggesting the prosecution be given a chance to establish an offence under section 336. Subsequently, a Division Bench of the High Court issued suo motu notice to the complainant and all the accused to show cause why the order of discharge should not be set aside. The High Court then reversed the orders passed by the Chief Presidency Magistrate.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused-appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the judgment and order of the Calcutta High Court in Criminal Revision No. 475 of 1967. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment and order, and restored the orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate.

directions: The judgment and order of the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 475 of 1967 are set aside.
The orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate dated March 20, and June 8, 1967 will stand restored.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with and setting aside the orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate which discharged the accused.

facts: The Chief Presidency Magistrate passed two orders discharging the accused in a case.
A Division Bench of the High Court, acting on its own initiative (suo motu), interfered with and set aside the Magistrate's orders.
Prior to the Magistrate's orders, a Single Judge of the same High Court had issued specific directions which limited the scope of the offenses the Magistrate was to consider.

The High Court's reasons for setting aside the discharge included that the discharge for non-payment of process fees was improper and that the discharge under Section 253(2) Cr.P.C. was not justified.
law: In a proper case, a High Court has the power to take action suo motu against orders passed by subordinate courts.
A Magistrate has the jurisdiction under Section 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code to discharge an accused if the charge is considered groundless, provided good reasons are given.
Subordinate courts are bound to follow the directions given to them by the High Court.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's Division Bench committed a "serious mistake" by ignoring the prior findings and clear directions given by a Single Judge of the same court.

The Chief Presidency Magistrate was correctly following the Single Judge's directions, which had essentially found that a case for the more serious offenses (ss. 337 and 338 I.P.C.) could not be upheld.
The Supreme Court reasoned that it was wrong for the Division Bench to criticize the Magistrate for adhering to these binding directions.

As an alternative reason, the Court stated that even if the Magistrate had to proceed with the trial for the more serious offenses, he had the jurisdiction under Section 253(2) Cr.P.C. to discharge the accused and had provided "good reasons" for doing so.

While acknowledging the High Court's general power to act suo motu, the Supreme Court determined that its interference in this specific instance was "not justified and was not warranted in the circumstances of the case."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the Magistrate's orders that had discharged the accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Magistrate had jurisdiction to permit the withdrawal of the complaint under Section 248 of the Criminal Procedure Code, treating the case as a summons case for an offence under Section 336 of the Indian Penal Code.

facts: The High Court had previously determined that the proceedings against the accused should continue only to inquire if an offence under Section 336 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) had been made out, rather than the originally alleged offences under Sections 337 and 338.
law: An inquiry for an offence under Section 336 of the IPC must follow the summons case procedure.
Section 248 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) allows a complainant to withdraw a complaint in a summons case, with the permission of the Magistrate.
application: The Court reasoned that since the case was to be treated as a summons case for an offence under Section 336 IPC, the provisions of Section 248 Cr.P.C. were applicable.
Under Section 248 Cr.P.C., the Court found that the Magistrate has "ample jurisdiction" to permit the complainant to withdraw the complaint.
The Court also noted that upon permitting such a withdrawal, the Magistrate is required to acquit the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Magistrate had the jurisdiction to permit the withdrawal of the complaint under Section 248 Cr.P.C. because the case was being treated as a summons case for an offence under Section 336 IPC. Therefore, the Magistrate's action was within his jurisdiction and could not be characterized as illegal or unjustified.

issue.issue_text: Whether, even if the proceedings were treated as a warrant case, the Magistrate had jurisdiction under Section 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code to discharge the accused.

facts: The case involved proceedings for offences under sections 337 and 338 of the Indian Penal Code, which required following the procedure for a warrant case.
The Magistrate discharged the accused under Section 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The High Court set aside the Magistrate's order, holding that a discharge under Section 253(2) was not justified in a warrant case.
law: The Court analyzed Section 253 of the Cr.P.C., which deals with the discharge of an accused.
Section 253(1) allows for discharge after all evidence has been taken.

Section 253(2) states: "Nothing in this section shall be deemed to prevent a Magistrate from discharging the accused at any previous stage of the case if, for reasons to be recorded by such Magistrate, he considers the charge to be groundless."
application: The Supreme Court held that Section 253(2) grants a Magistrate "ample jurisdiction" to discharge an accused even when following the warrant case procedure.
The Court clarified that the power under subsection (2) can be exercised "at any previous stage of the case" and is not barred by the procedure outlined in subsection (1).
The only condition for exercising this power is that the Magistrate must record reasons for finding the charge to be groundless.
In this specific case, the Court noted that the Magistrate had acted under Section 253(2) and had given good reasons for the discharge.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Magistrate had the jurisdiction under Section 253(2) of the Cr.P.C. to discharge the accused, even though the proceedings were being treated as a warrant case. Therefore, the High Court's interference with the Magistrate's order was not justified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with and setting aside the orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate which discharged the accused.
appellant_arguments: There was no justification for the High Court to interfere suo motu with the orders passed by the Chief Presidency Magistrate discharging the accused.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's interference was justified because the Magistrate's discharge orders were improper.
The discharge of some accused under s. 204(3) Cr. P.C. for non-payment of process fees was improper as no such fee is required for cognizable offenses.
The discharge of the accused under s. 253(2) Cr. P.C. was not justified as the proceeding under s. 338 I.P.C. was a warrant case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Magistrate had jurisdiction to permit the withdrawal of the complaint under Section 248 of the Criminal Procedure Code, treating the case as a summons case for an offence under Section 336 of the Indian Penal Code.
appellant_arguments: Following the High Court's (Single Judge) earlier order, the proceedings were to continue only to inquire if an offence under s. 336 I.P.C. was made out.
A trial for an offence under s. 336 I.P.C. is a summons case, which gives the Magistrate jurisdiction to act accordingly.
respondent_arguments: The proceeding was initiated for an offence under s. 338 I.P.C., which is a warrant case, and it should have continued to be treated as such.
The Magistrate was not justified in treating the matter as a summons case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether, even if the proceedings were treated as a warrant case, the Magistrate had jurisdiction under Section 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code to discharge the accused.
appellant_arguments: The discharge under s. 253(2) Cr. P.C. was justified because the complainant was not present and was not serious about proceeding with the complaint, as evidenced by several defaults.
respondent_arguments: The discharge orders under s. 253(2) Cr. P.C. were not justified, as held by the High Court, because the proceeding was a warrant case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In a proper case, a High Court can take action suo motu against the orders passed by subordinate courts without being moved by any party.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court held that the High Court's Division Bench was not justified in interfering with the orders of the Chief Presidency Magistrate which discharged the accused. The Court found that, considering the matter from any point of view and under the specific circumstances of the case, the Magistrate had acted within his jurisdiction, and the High Court's suo motu interference was not warranted.
legal_tests_applied: Jurisdiction of a Magistrate under Section 253(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code: This sub-section provides a Magistrate with ample jurisdiction to discharge an accused in a warrant case at any previous stage of the case for reasons deemed sufficient, and sub-section (1) does not operate as a bar to this power.
Jurisdiction of a Magistrate under Section 248 of the Criminal Procedure Code: In a summons case, this section gives the Magistrate jurisdiction to permit a complainant to withdraw the complaint.

Propriety of High Court's Suo Motu Interference: While the High Court has the power to take action suo motu against orders of subordinate courts, the exercise of this power must be justified by the circumstances of the case.
why_respondent_won: The Magistrate had jurisdiction to discharge the accused under Section 253(2) Cr.P.C. even if the matter was treated as a warrant case. The court noted that this sub-section gives ample jurisdiction to discharge an accused at any previous stage and that the Magistrate had given good reasons for his order.

Alternatively, based on a prior High Court order that effectively limited the inquiry to a potential offence under s. 336 I.P.C., the Magistrate was justified in adopting the summons case procedure. Under that procedure, the Magistrate had jurisdiction under s. 248 Cr.P.C. to permit the complainant to withdraw the complaint.

The High Court's interference with the Magistrate's orders was not justified or warranted in the circumstances of the case. The Supreme Court found that, viewing the matter from either the warrant case or summons case perspective, the Magistrate's actions were legally sound.
policy_considerations: The Court affirmed the principle that the High Court has the power to take action suo motu against the orders of subordinate courts to ensure justice, but clarified that this power should only be exercised in proper cases and was not justified in the present circumstances.
